articles.title: Rahm Emanuel accuses anti-Israel Dems of having no Middle East plan besides cutting funding to Jewish state
articles.excerpt: In an interview with Fox News Digital, former US Ambassador Rahm Emanuel called out anti-Israel Democrats for not having a broader foreign policy plan besides cutting weapons funding to the Jewish Sta...
articles.body_text:
In an interview with Fox News Digital, former US Ambassador Rahm Emanuel called out anti-Israel Democrats for not having a broader foreign policy plan besides cutting weapons funding to the Jewish State.

AUSTIN — Former U.S. Ambassador Rahm Emanuel is challenging the anti-Israel wing of his party, accusing Democrats of not having a broader policy on the Middle East besides cutting weapons funding.

"I'm interested in being as vigorous and strong about what a security peace agreement would bring to both the United States and to Israel and to the alliance and how you can build on that," Emanuel told Fox News Digital in an interview during the Texas Tribune Festival.

"Now, people will criticize it. Fine. You got to tell me your plan. And your plan can't just be we're going to cut off funding for weapons. What's your peace idea? What's your security idea? What's the economic package? I've laid out mine," the Democrat continued. "I'm looking forward to anybody else wanting to run. Because guess what? The White House comes with more than just the Oval Office. It comes with a place called the Situation Room. And you better know your way around it."

RAHM EMANUEL EXPRESSES SUPPORT FOR ABDUL EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE

Former U.S. Ambassador Rahm Emanuel speaks at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin, Texas on Wednesday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Joseph A. Wulfsohn/Fox News Digital)

Emanuel, who is openly mulling a 2028 presidential run, gave a lengthy policy speech at Israel's Tel Aviv University in July, saying the country's alliance with the U.S. is "at a crossroads" due to the Jewish state's increasing unpopularity with Americans and declaring Israel "has never been more strategically isolated."

Democrats, in particular, have soured on Israel far more than Republicans. A Gallup study from February showed 65% of Democrats are sympathetic to Palestinians in the ongoing Middle East conflict, while just 17% are sympathetic to Israel, down from peak support in 2014 at 58%. Meanwhile, 70% of Republicans still side with Israel versus the 13% that are sympathetic to Palestinians, though support for the Jewish state among Republicans is still down from its peak of 87% in 2018.

RAHM EMANUEL TOUTS WHAT SEPARATES HIMSELF FROM OTHER DEMS AS HE MULLS 2028 PRESIDENTIAL BID

Rahm Emanuel, a potential Democratic presidential candidate and longtime defender of Israel, speaks at Tel Aviv University, Israel, Wednesday, July 8, 2026. (Ariel Schalit/AP Photos)

When asked whether Jewish Zionists were still welcomed in his party and whether he still calls himself one, Emanuel laughed.

"Look, as I said then, I believe in the alliance," Emanuel responded. "I believe in the United States' interest in the alliance. But the path we're on is unsustainable. And I believe I'm being honest and bringing candor to it. And I think I bring a level of authenticity having worked on both the peace process and also the security of an ally, the state of Israel. But you can't sustain something that doesn't have the support of the American people."

The former Chicago mayor also stressed he's "not interested in fighting a third war" in the Middle East.

Emanuel also served three terms in Congress representing Illinois, chaired the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee when Democrats retook Congress in 2006, and was President Barack Obama's first White House chief of staff. After two terms as mayor of Chicago from 2011 to 2019, he served in the Biden administration as U.S. Ambassador to Japan.

RAHM EMANUEL LAYS OUT FIVE-POINT ETHICS PLAN, SAYS DEMOCRATS SHOULD LEARN FROM GOP-LED STATES ON EDUCATION

American support for Israel under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reached new lows, particularly with Democrats. (Ronen Zvulun/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Fox News' Brian Flood contributed to this report.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: What is ‘Herod’s Pool’, and why is Israel developing it in the West Bank?
articles.excerpt:
Israel says that work has begun on a development project around an outdoor pool in the occupied West Bank filled after settlers illegally diverted water from a Palestinian village over the summer.

In...
articles.body_text:
Israel says that work has begun on a development project around an outdoor pool in the occupied West Bank filled after settlers illegally diverted water from a Palestinian village over the summer.

Instead of restoring the water to the village of Fasayil, near Jericho, Israeli authorities are working to formalise what has now been termed “Herod’s Pool”, named after an ancient Jewish king.

On Sunday, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a far-right settler, announced that “development and preservation” of Herod’s Pool had commenced, connecting it to a larger project to “strengthen [Israel’s] hold” on and preserve historical sites.

“The Settlement Revolution continues!” he declared in a social media post that carried an image of workers and wheelbarrows near the site.

The announcement follows Smotrich’s June pledge of more than three million shekels (almost $1m) to develop the site, even though the pool sits on privately-owned Palestinian land belonging to a farmer.

The illegal diversion of water to the pool is part of Israel’s monopolisation of water resources in the occupied West Bank’s fertile Jordan Valley.

It also marks the latest Israeli seizure of Palestinian land in the name of archaeological heritage.

Here’s what we know about the Herod’s Pool project.

Herod’s Pool is the name Israeli settlers have given an ancient reservoir that lies in the Palestinian village of Fasayil. It is named after Herod the Great, a Jewish king from the first century BC.

The reservoir sits next to a natural spring.

Although settlers claim it once belonged to King Herod, archaeologists have not established when the pool was built. Alon Arad, executive director of Emek Shaveh, an Israeli NGO that defends cultural heritage rights and monitors the political use of archaeology, told the Reuters news agency that the pool’s origins are unclear.

“We see in many cases the use of archaeology … to create this feeling that the West Bank is exclusively Jewish,” he said.

Israeli politicians and settlers have also sought greater Israeli control over “Solomon’s Pools”, three ancient reservoirs in Bethlehem governorate, which have been used by Palestinians for generations.

Palestinians say the targeting of their water sources is part of a comprehensive plan to seize the resources of the occupied West Bank and force them off their land.

The reservoir sits on land belonging to Palestinian farmer Saad Nemer and his family. Nemer says that his grandfather purchased the property more than a century ago. Israeli-issued documentation and older title records reviewed by Reuters support the family’s ownership claim.

Nemer said that settlers had been repeatedly redirecting water from his farm to swim in the pool. He explained that settlers had stolen his irrigation pipeline for the task, and over time the theft had left his farmland scorched and his greenhouses empty.

Nemer also said that settlers had threatened him and beat one of his employees.

The Israeli military body that administers the occupied West Bank, COGAT, has acknowledged that the water was diverted “without authorisation” and said it would investigate, even as Smotrich and other Israeli politicians celebrate the pool.

Nemer told The New York Times that he had been informed by COGAT that his water would be restored, but said it returned for only one day before being cut off again. He is now fearful of approaching the reservoir to reconnect his pipeline due to settler violence.

While there is no proven link to Herod, the name features prominently in Israeli heritage projects across the occupied West Bank, which Israel refers to as “Judea and Samaria” in an attempt to separate it from its Palestinian population.

Critics, including archaeological rights groups, say such projects are increasingly being used to extend Israeli control over Palestinian land and heritage sites.

There is Herodium, a sprawling hilltop structure south of Jerusalem, said to be the ruins of a fortress the king erected. It has been under Israeli control for decades and operates as a national park, despite Palestinian protests that it is part of their heritage.

In Sebastia – ancient Samaria – Israel has dedicated large amounts of funding since 2023 to excavate the city’s archaeological park and develop it as an Israeli “national park“, usurping Palestinians who have long showcased the archaeological ruins as part of their history.

Israeli Minister of Heritage Amichai Eliyahu, who himself lives in an illegal West Bank settlement, has said it would be “first and foremost a Jewish heritage site”. His office cited excavation of “the magnificent Roman city built by King Herod” when describing the archaeological periods the project intends to expose.

The Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron – where Israel has repeatedly restricted Muslim access – stands on land considered to be Prophet Abraham’s burial place by Muslims and Jews. Part of it is believed to have been built during the Herodian era.

In 2017, UNESCO recognised Hebron’s Old City as a Palestinian heritage site, and warned that it was endangered by Israeli settler encroachments.

Ahead of UNESCO’s decision, prominent Hebron settler Yishai Fleisher – who has served as an adviser to Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir – objected to the designation on the grounds that it was “built by a Jewish king”, referring to Herod.

articles.title: Sass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65
articles.excerpt:
Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol

Sass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock scene in the...
articles.body_text:
Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol

Sass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock scene in the 1990s before starring as a judge on Canadian Idol, has died aged 65.

No cause of death has been given. A statement on social media said she died on 2 October “surrounded by her loving family … She remains in our hearts, an inimitable force of nature. An irreplaceable being of light and joy!”

Born in Birmingham, England, in 1960, Jordan moved to Montreal as a child when her French academic father took a position at the city’s Concordia University. She began performing in her teens, and by her 20s was recording with a range of Montreal acts: she wrote a song for singer Michael Breen that became a Canadian Top 40 hit.

By 1988 she was signed to Atlantic Records, who released her debut album Tell Somebody, with two singles – the title track and Double Trouble – charting just outside the Canadian Top 10. The following year she won a Juno (the Canadian equivalent of the Grammys) for most promising female vocalist.

Her 1992 album Racine contained four Canadian Top 20 hits and, coupled with a move to Los Angeles, a new label in RCA, and an appearance on the bestselling soundtrack to The Bodyguard broke Jordan into a wider US market. Sun’s Gonna Rise, from 1994 album Rats, became her only US Hot 100 hit, and her biggest hit in Canada, reaching No 7. Taylor Hawkins, later the drummer for Foo Fighters, was her live drummer during this period.

Her RCA deal ended and Jordan later voiced disappointment in the glossy sound of her next couple of albums, but her career received a boost from being a judge on the six seasons of TV talent show Canadian Idol, and she returned to recording with 2006’s You Get What You Give. In 2001 she also performed as Janis Joplin in the off-Broadway musical Love, Janis.

She later embraced a bluesier sound, with 2020 album Rebel Moon Blues reaching the top five of the US blues chart, followed by her most recent studio recording, 2022’s Bitches Blues.

In September, Jordan cancelled tour dates, citing “a serious medical condition”.

articles.title: US air force removes all bombers from British military base RAF Fairford
articles.excerpt:
A Rockwell B1 Lancer heavy bomber takes off to depart for home at RAF Fairford on Sunday

The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the UK military base at the centre of an incident b...
articles.body_text:
A Rockwell B1 Lancer heavy bomber takes off to depart for home at RAF Fairford on Sunday

The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the UK military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.

A statement from a Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.

US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Whitehall sources have not disputed the decision from Washington was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.

The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

The UK's Ministry of Defence has not commented.

Tracking websites showed B-1 bombers flying out of RAF Fairford on Sunday.

The New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.

The newspaper wrote the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.

The planes reportedly took off while aerial refueling aircraft were still being scrambled to support their flights to the US.

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.

RAF Fairford, nearby the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

The withdrawal of the bombers comes as the US tries to recover from the damage inflicted on its aircraft by Iranian precision strikes.

It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year.

But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will remove a foothold for the country outside of continental Europe.

Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, said the decision to move the planes out of RAF Fairford was a "prudent decision".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced any more, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it, from all sorts of threats."

Cohen added that the consequences of the decision "raises the cost of striking Iran", because military aircraft will now either have to fly from the US or from another base in Europe.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Days after the incident, and before the arrest of the sixth man, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor".

Rubio did not provide further details - saying at the time he was limited on what he could say on air.

US President Donald Trump separately said he was "surprised" the five men had been released on bail.

"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

Many B-1 bombers flown from the UK were armed with precision-guided "bunker busting" bombs, with thicker casings to penetrate hardened or buried targets such as weapons stores.

They also carried air-to-surface missiles used against more heavily defended targets deeper inside Iran.

Each bombing mission, depending on the location of the target, would likely have taken around 12 to 15 hours in total there and back, with air-to-air refuelling both ways.

The Pentagon has stressed its bombing aircraft remain able to conduct missions "anywhere, anytime", including through "operations that launch and recover from the continental United States".

RAF Fairford base was occupied by USAF Strategic Air Command during the Cold War and later the first Gulf War in 1991.

The base remains owned by the Ministry of Defence but is operated by the USAF under agreements between the UK and US governments.

The base regularly hosts deployments of long-range American aircraft, including B-52 bombers and U-2 reconnaissance aircraft, and has played a role in recent operations linked to tensions in the Middle East.

B-52 bombers were most recently used in March following a decision by former UK prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to allow the US to use UK bases - including RAF Fairford - for "defensive" strikes on Iranian capabilities.

Conflict was sparked across the Middle East after the US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February.

Iran responded by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf.

articles.title: Shadow chancellor to address Tory conference as he claims slashing red tape could cut cost of new houses by £50,000 – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Andrew Griffith makes speech today as Reform UK accuses party of copying policies they ‘announced weeks and months ago’

Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England

The Conservat...
articles.body_text:
Andrew Griffith makes speech today as Reform UK accuses party of copying policies they ‘announced weeks and months ago’

Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England

The Conservatives would legislate to force the Scottish government to allow a new power station to be built in Scotland, Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, is saying.

Bowie is speaking at the conference this morning and, in comments released in advance, he says:

double quotation markThe SNP’s effective ban on new nuclear energy in Scotland flies in the face of common-sense.

No part of Great Britain should be missing out on plans for new nuclear renewal.

That is why I am delighted to announce that the Conservatives will look to see how we can legislate to deliver new nuclear energy in Scotland.

The SNP’s luddite approach is costing jobs in Scotland, harming our energy security and ending Scotland’s rich and powerful association with the nuclear industry.

The SNP government in power in Scotland is opposed to building nuclear power stations.

New vetting rules for Conservative candidates – sometimes described as a purge of moderates – are not a “purity test” and the party is a “broad church”, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said this morning.

As the Press Association reports, asked whether Kemi Badenoch’s idea of a model Tory MP would mean that former politicians like Ken Clarke may not qualify under the new rules, he told Times Radio:

double quotation markLook, we are a broad church; it’s not a purity test.

But when people vote for our party, they often, as they did previously, they like the things that we stand for, but they were extremely frustrated with our inability to deliver those in government.

So we do have to learn from that … It does have to be different next time. A greater degree of preparedness, a team that’s working together, united to deliver things, and making sure we’ve got the right.

Yesterday Penny Mordaunt, the former cabinet minister, said that she had been appoved for the candidates list. But Grant Shapps, another former cabinet minister who would like to return to parliament, seems likely to be blocked.

While the Tories debate the economy, Andy Burnham is hosting an away-day for his cabinet at Chequers, Andrew McDonald reports in his London Playbook briefing for Politico. He says:

double quotation markOne person tells Playbook there’ll be a session on the upcoming 10-year plan, which is due by the end of the year. Another person says much of the away day is about planning how to tackle the next three months, which may excite some of those Tories in Birmingham still arguing that a December election (?!) is a possibility. Long-term and short-term, there are loads of policy questions still to flesh out within Burnham’s sweepy vision. Cabinet ministers in Liverpool last week were waxing lyrical about Burnham’s openness and interest in their briefs as compared to the previous regime, so there’s a chance some of them might get something useful out of all this face time with the PM.

Sir Ephraim Mirvis, the chief rabbi, issued this statement last night criticising the Green party over its vote to say “Zionism is racism”. He describes it as “poisonous antisemitism’.

double quotation markEmerging from our festival of Simchat Torah tonight, I was appalled to hear that the Green Party had passed its ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion earlier today.

It was the Soviet Union which first promoted the dangerous lie that Zionism is racism.

The UN adopted it, but was then shamed into revoking it.

Those in the Green Party and beyond who resurrect this discredited and dangerous slander should not imagine that history will judge them kindly.

All decent people will see this for what it is: poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain.

I would encourage those who wish to understand what Zionism truly is to read my essay from 2024.

The Labour party has issued a detailed response to the proposals announced by Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, today. (See 8.08am.) In part, Labour is saying the problems Griffith raises are being addressed. But mostly it is saying the Tories have no credibility on these issues because they ignored them or allowed them to get worse, when they were in power.

On the Environment Agency and Natural England

Labour says it is already making these quangos more effective. It says the Environment Agency “now has both the officers on the frontline and the powers to go after illegal waste criminals” and the rules have been changed to reduce the role of Natural England in planning.

On getting rid of the EPR (extended producer responsibility)

Labour says EPR was a scheme “first announced by Theresa May and kept in place by successive Conservative governments, including ones served by members of the current shadow cabinet”.

Griffith is complaining in particular about the impact on the glass industry, because under pEPR (packaging extended producer responsibility) costs are higher for glass bottles than plastic bottles. Labour says ministers are “alive to pressures on the glass industry” and are working on a solution.

Labour says the Tories did not build these when they were in power.

Labour says the length of the tax code “increased massively” when the Tories were in office.

Labour says the average first-time buyer deposit in England rose from £28,770 when the Tories took office in 2010 to £55,372 when they left. It also says that, by 2024, 31% of first-time buyers needed a gift or loan from family or friends to pay a deposit. Labour announced a Your First Home scheme at conference to help first-time buyers, it says.

Labour points out that Griffith opposed a second runway at Gatwick, near his constituency.

This is what the Tories are saying in their overnight news release about their plans to cut regulation affecting building on why they believe their measures could cut the cost of a new house by £50,000.

double quotation markThe Conservatives have already pledged to scrap stamp duty on the family home, giving people a leg up onto the housing ladder. Now we are announcing radical supply-side reforms that will ensure the homes we need actually get built.

We will scrap unnecessary net-zero housing red tape that is stopping developers from building and driving up the cost of housing. We will ditch the Future Homes Standard and Part L of the Housing Regulations. All in all, we will cut the cost of delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000.

And here is the longer version. (Bold type from the original.)

double quotation markIdeological net zero rules alone have added more than £30,000 to the cost of building a new home. Local Government viability assessments show that Net Zero rules add tens of thousands of pounds to the cost of building a new home. For instance, Birmingham City Council assessed that improved efficiency, heat pumps and solar panels increase the cost of a new detached home by as much as £30,789. The London Borough of Lewisham estimated that these rules would increase build costs by 15 per cent. (Birmingham City Council, Net Zero Plan Supporting Evidence Report, 7 September 2023, link, Lewisham Council, Viability Study 2022, 17 May 2022, link.)

These costs can be even higher as local and regional authorities often gold-plate these rules, imposing extra cost on developers. For instance, Policy SI2 (C) in the London Plan 2021 requires a 35 per cent uplift on energy efficiency beyond the national Building Regulations for major developments. (Mayor of London, The London Plan, March 2021, link.)

Other mandated changes are adding thousands in costs:

Government proposals on water efficiency are estimated to cost an additional £3,100 per home. (Home Builders Federation, The Viability Crunch, 1 May 2026 link.)

Requirements for EV chargers on all new residential buildings are increasing costs by £870 per property. (Home Builders Federation, The Viability Crunch, 1 May 2026 link.)

Accessibility standards introduced in 2022 have gold-plated requirements for wider internal staircases and level thresholds for entry to properties in new builds, which are estimated to have added £1,800 to the cost of building a home. (Home Builders Federation, The Viability Crunch, 1 May 2026 link.)

Additional Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) rules are adding £5,700 to the cost of construction:

Local authorities are imposing additional local rules significantly exceeding the national 10 per cent target for BNG. For instance:

More than a dozen local authorities require BNG of 20 per cent or more (as of January 2025). (Urbanist Architecture, BNG requirements for planning, 27 January 2025, link.)

Tower Hamlets in 2025 proposed a 30 per cent BNG target. (London Borough of Tower Hamlets Council, New Local Plan, June 2025, link.)

Last night Israel’s foreign affairs ministry said that Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, has been banned from the country following his party conference voting for a motion saying “Zionism is racism”.

The motion was “a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”, the ministry said. It went on:

double quotation markTherefore, as a first step, foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided this evening to declare Green party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel.

Here is Peter Walker’s full story on the Green party vote.

Good morning. Yesterday Kemi Badenoch published a tract setting out the principles that a Conservative government would follow in office. It was presented as Thatcherism revived for the 21st century, and a key theme was that government should leave wealth creation up to business, and not get in the way with red tape.

Today Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, is presenting a plan that illustrates what this would mean in practice. Normally, at party conference, ministers and shadow ministers put out a press release in advance of their speeches highlighting just one headline policy idea, with perhaps one or two associated policies.

Overnight Griffith has published what is practically a manifesto. The press release alone runs to almost 5,000 words. Jessica Elgot had the task of reading them all for us yesterday and here is her write-up.

She has led her story on the plan to get rid of two environment quangos, the Environment Agency and Natural England.

But there are plenty of other proposals in the package too, including:

-Getting rid of net zero regulations and other planning laws, including section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy, that put up the cost of housebuilding.

-Getting rid of the EPR (extended producer responsibility), a law intended to make producers liable for waste disposal costs. The Tories call it the “grocery tax”.

-Leaving the Aarhus convention, an international treaty giving the public access to information relating to environmental decision-making. The Tories claim this enables the “lawfare hindering every major infrastructure project in this country”.

-Speeding up the delivery of more nuclear power stations.

The Tories claim the plans relating to housebuilding would “cut up to an estimated £50,000 off the price of a new home”.

There is more detail in what Griffith is proposing, and there is clearly a lot to discuss. Labour and Reform UK have both responded overnight – but taking different lines of attack.

Labour has said that Griffith has no credibility on these topics. In an overnight statement, Bridget Phillipson, the party chair, said:

double quotation markTrusting the co-author of Liz Truss’ disastrous mini-Budget with Tory plans on the economy and housing is like asking an arsonist to run the fire service. Kemi Badenoch is once again demonstrating her appalling lack of judgement.

The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn.

But Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader and business spokesperson, says that Griffith is copying ideas that his party has already adopted. He says:

double quotation markTories pledge to scrap some costs regulations and taxes they put in place!

They are copying Reform policies we announced weeks and months ago!

They are trying to fix problems they created 😡

One of the themes emerging at this conference is that, while there is far less talk of some sort of Tory/Reform UK pact than there was a year ago, the policy overlap continues. Yesterday the Conservatives announced two other proposals (excluding foreigners from the student loan scheme, and reducing aid spending to just £1bn a year) that were little more than cut-and-paste versions of Reform UK pledges.

9.45am: Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, speaks at the conference on the main stage (the smaller of the two halls the Tories are using at this conference for speeches). The other main morning speakers are Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, at 10.30am; Damian Hinds, the shadow health secretary, at 11.15am; and Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, and Laura Trott, after 12.15pm.

12.14pm: Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, speaking in the fanzone area on the Conservative’s rural vision.

2pm: Griffith takes part in “meet the team” event in the symphony hall (the conference stage being used for larger events) with Richard Fuller, chief secretary to the Treasury, Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, and Julia Lopez, the acting shadow business secretary.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Coach services could be cut due to record diesel prices, UK operators warn
articles.excerpt:
Rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business, threatening school transport, firms say

Coach operators have said record diesel prices could force cuts to services including school t...
articles.body_text:
Rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business, threatening school transport, firms say

Coach operators have said record diesel prices could force cuts to services including school transport, as hauliers warn rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business.

The average price of diesel on UK forecourts hit a fresh record of more than £2 a litre last week, as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global fuel supplies.

Alison Edwards, the director of policy at the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT), said the cost of fuel had “surged this year to unsustainable levels, pushing coach operators’ already tight margins to breaking point”.

“It is time for urgent action,” she said. “Without intervention, soaring prices will mean difficult decisions on the availability of services, including home-to-school transport, and the viability of businesses.”

Edwards said 85% of independent coach operators are family businesses, and called on the government to provide temporary support with the cost of diesel, adding that the industry “needs help”.

Local bus operators in England have already received help with fuel costs via subsidies to help cover running costs. Coach companies, which say they carry out a similar role, have received no equivalent support.

Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association (RHA), said the haulage sector was under similar strain. “Businesses in our sector operate on slim profit margins, typically about 2%, so the continuing high fuel costs are a huge challenge for us,” he said.

He said hauliers were now paying an extra £350 a week for each truck compared with before the Iran war. “It’s just unsustainable,” he said. “If haulage, coach and van operators can’t pass these costs on, they struggle, and we’ve seen hundreds of transport businesses going bust already this year.”

Hauliers are calling for a pause on planned fuel duty rises, and a rebate to help offset the cost of diesel. The RAC motoring organisation has called for the government to expand its 5p cut in fuel duty, which has already been extended until the end of the year.

Rhys Hackling, the managing director of Direct Connect Logistics, said the impact on his own business had been “absolutely enormous”.

The company runs 22 lorries out of Oxfordshire, Northamptonshire and Warrington, transporting goods ranging from supermarket products to live events equipment. He said the company was spending much more on fuel compared with last year: “We normally spend about £50,000 a month on fuel … it’s now knocking on £65,000.”

Many hauliers work on fixed contracts with customers, Hackling said, meaning rising fuel costs squeeze or wipe out their margins entirely. “If these events continue, then it’s going to put a lot of haulage firms out of business,” he said.

“There’s less confidence in the market, so there are fewer jobs, and that means the work dries up very, very quickly. Somebody somewhere is having to pay for this, whether it’s the haulage firm or whether it’s the consumer.”

In a move offering some hope that fuel prices might ease, leaders of G7 nations said on Friday that they would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles.

The announcement was partly in response to Donald Trump suggesting he might introduce a ban on diesel exports after the rise in sales to overseas buyers pushed US prices to record highs.

It appears to have averted the threat, which could have pushed diesel prices even higher in the UK, since Britain relies on the US for about a third of its diesel imports and does not refine enough to meet demand on its own.

The benchmark Brent crude oil price declined by nearly 1% on Monday to just over $101 a barrel.

The transport minister, Keir Mather, has said the UK’s fuel supply is “inherently resilient” and that people “shouldn’t be concerned about shortages”.

articles.title: How Spain's housing crisis has resulted in an early general election
articles.excerpt: Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez confirmed Spain will be heading to the polls on 29 November, after Sanchez's Socialist party, which is currently heading a minority government, failed to pass housing refo...
articles.body_text:
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez confirmed Spain will be heading to the polls on 29 November, after Sanchez's Socialist party, which is currently heading a minority government, failed to pass housing reforms in the Spanish Congress.

Sanchez faces an uphill battle in his bid for re-election with polls showing Sánchez's Socialist party is trailing the conservative People's Party - which many expect to attempt to form a government with the far-right Vox.

In his statement announcing the election, Sanchez warned Spaniards about what he called the "extreme-right wave" being seen in other countries and said Spain should continue to be a global example of "peace, feminism and prosperity".

Follow the BBC's live coverage following Sanchez's announcement.

articles.title: Formula One to probe software bug behind Bahrain GP chaos in Sepang
articles.excerpt: Formula One’s governing body has promised a full investigation into a software bug that caused chaos and forced the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted, with drivers feeling like...
articles.body_text:
Formula One’s governing body has promised a full investigation into a software bug that caused chaos and forced the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted, with drivers feeling like they were in battery-powered cars made of Lego.

Ferrari’s seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull’s four-time champion and eventual race winner Max Verstappen were among several affected by the glitch on a formation lap after torrential rain and a long delay at Malaysia’s steamy Sepang circuit on Sunday.

Verstappen compared the experience to a “Lego race” held at Silverstone before the British Grand Prix while Hamilton, the sport’s most successful driver of all time, had to stop his car on track and restart it in what he said was a career first.

The episode was the latest in a difficult first season for the new era of cars and engines, with drivers at the pinnacle of motorsport unhappy since the opening race with the power units’ increased electrical component and the need for energy management.

FIA said afterwards that “an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars”.

“As a result, the FIA technical department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race.

“This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue.”

The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis told reporters the lack of preseason testing in wet conditions had played a part in the chaos.

“Some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely,” he said. “That bug prevented the power from being redeployed, and for the cars to start again.

“I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time, and not have such a situation.”

Sepang was the first race weekend of the season with wet conditions, although the track dried during the race.

“Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time,” Tombazis said.

articles.title: Wall Street has a new rival, and it's deep in the heart of this southern state
articles.excerpt:
Texas Stock Exchange strategic adviser and former Rep. Jeb Hensarling breaks down why he believes the Lone Star State is emerging as the nation's next financial powerhouse.

DALLAS — Wall Street has l...
articles.body_text:
Texas Stock Exchange strategic adviser and former Rep. Jeb Hensarling breaks down why he believes the Lone Star State is emerging as the nation's next financial powerhouse.

DALLAS — Wall Street has long been the undisputed home of American finance. Now, one southern state wants a seat at the table.

The Texas Stock Exchange is at the center of an ambitious effort to transform the Lone Star State into America's next financial powerhouse, challenging the long-standing dominance of the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq while fueling the rise of what's become affectionately known as "Y'all Street."

The Dallas-based exchange plans to provide companies with another venue to list their shares and raise capital, with supporters betting it will help establish Texas as America's next financial frontier.

ONE SOUTHERN STATE'S RISE IS MAKING IT AMERICA'S NEW 'ECONOMIC CENTER OF GRAVITY'

Texas has attracted a wave of corporate relocations and business investment in recent years, helping fuel its emergence as a growing financial hub. (Shelby Tauber/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

Former Rep. Jeb Hensarling, R-Texas, a strategic advisor and member of the Texas Stock Exchange, believes the shift is already underway.

"Texas is really becoming the economic center of gravity in America," Hensarling told Fox News Digital during an interview at the Texas Stock Exchange's headquarters.

"As New York is increasingly shoving capital out, Texas is saying, 'You're welcome here,'" he said. "We put out the welcome mat, whereas New York, capital isn't really made to feel at home, and capital wants to go where it's made to feel at home."

Hensarling argued that years of pro-business policies have helped transform Texas into more than just an attractive place to operate a company.

GOV ABBOTT EXTENDS OFF-RAMP FOR NY BILLIONAIRES FLEEING MAMDANI'S POLICIES

The Texas Stock Exchange is headquartered in Dallas and aims to compete with the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. (Al Drago/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

"Texas has been a great place to do business for decades, but increasingly it's a great place to headquarter your business," he said. "Over the last couple of legislative sessions, because of laws passed, it's a great place to incorporate your business."

"The last piece of that puzzle was the Texas Stock Exchange," Hensarling said. "It's now making Texas the best place to list your company and to go public."

BILLIONS IN TAXPAYER INCOME ARE LEAVING TWO ICONIC STATES — AS A NEW ECONOMIC MAP EMERGES

The Texas Stock Exchange has already announced primary listings from companies including Energy Transfer, Dillard's, Sunoco and Texas Capital Bank. (Al Drago/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The exchange is part of a broader wave of investment flowing into Texas. In recent years, major corporations have moved their headquarters to the state, while financial giants including Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab and Bank of America have expanded their Texas operations.

Supporters say those moves reflect a larger migration of businesses and capital away from traditional financial centers toward states with lower taxes and lighter regulation.

Critics, however, note that New York remains the country's dominant financial hub by a wide margin, with the world's largest stock exchange, major investment banks and deep capital markets.

THIS STATE ISN'T JUST GROWING — ITS ECONOMY IS GETTING RICHER PER RESIDENT

Supporters have dubbed Dallas "Y'all Street" as Texas pushes to become a larger player in American finance with a new stock exchange and a growing concentration of financial firms. (Al Drago/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Whether "Y'all Street" can truly rival Wall Street remains an open question.

But with a new stock exchange, an influx of corporate headquarters and some of the nation's biggest financial firms expanding in Dallas, Texas is making its boldest bid yet to challenge Wall Street's dominance.

Hensarling believes the trajectory is clear.

"Texas is really becoming the economic center of gravity in America," he said.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launches legal action against police over Epstein raids
articles.excerpt:
Former prince to challenge whether Thames Valley police acted lawfully over searches relating to his arrest

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action against Thames Valley police to challenge the l...
articles.body_text:
Former prince to challenge whether Thames Valley police acted lawfully over searches relating to his arrest

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action against Thames Valley police to challenge the legality of search warrants that led to his arrest earlier this year, a judicial spokesperson has said.

A private high court hearing is due to take place before Mr Justice Hilliard on Thursday to determine whether documents related to the the former Duke of York’s call for a judicial review can be made public; with Thames Valley police in opposition.

The legal fight stems from the issuing of warrants by an Old Bailey judge that allowed police to raid Mountbatten-Windsor’s residence on the Sandringham estate, and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files.

A high court judge subsequently granted him permission to challenge the legality of the force’s actions over the searches.

According to the Daily Telegraph, which first reported Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal challenge, it represented the first time a member of the royal family had challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.

Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on his 66th birthday in relation to allegations that when he was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.

Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with the late financier.

Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on 19 February and interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.

Misconduct in public office can cover a wide range of conduct, including sharing confidential financial information, financial misconduct, wilful neglect of duty and sexual misconduct. It also covers corruption and improper interference, conflict of interest, perverting the course of justice, dishonesty or fraudulent conduct, and misconduct leading to personal gain.

Thames Valley police said: “Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”

Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for comment.

articles.title: America must defend our digital infrastructure, here and overseas, to win the next war
articles.excerpt:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on Republicans testing Senate Democrats with a data center pricing bill on 'America Reports.'

For most of American history, nati...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram has the latest on Republicans testing Senate Democrats with a data center pricing bill on 'America Reports.'

For most of American history, national defense has been understood geographically. There was American territory and foreign territory, borders to defend, military installations to protect and American forces stationed around the world. Even as warfare evolved, the basic concept remained relatively simple: the United States had physical assets that needed protection from foreign adversaries.

Technology has fundamentally changed that calculation. Today, some of the most important assets supporting America's economy, military and national security do not fit neatly within traditional definitions of territory or defense infrastructure. They are data centers, cloud-computing systems, telecommunications networks and other digital infrastructure that may be privately owned and located thousands of miles from the United States.

The border of the next war may not be a line on a map. It may be a data center.

OUR ENEMIES FOUND A WEAKNESS IN ESSENTIAL TECHNOLOGY. WE MUST FIX IT … FAST

The recent conflict with Iran should force Washington to take that possibility seriously. In March, Iranian strikes damaged Amazon Web Services data centers and infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, disrupting cloud infrastructure and creating problems with power and connectivity. Reuters reported that the damage contributed to service disruptions and an extended recovery process. Then, in April, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps publicly claimed that it had targeted an Amazon cloud-computing facility in Bahrain.

Aftermath of an Iranian missile strike on a Navy 5th Fleet installation in Bahrain is shown above. Iran also attacked an Amazon AWS facility there. (Stringer/Anadolu via Getty Images)

That distinction is important. This was not simply a commercial facility caught in the crossfire. Iran publicly identified American commercial computing infrastructure as a target.

8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS

That should be a warning for Washington. American power increasingly depends on infrastructure that is privately operated and, in some cases, located outside our borders. The military relies on commercial technology and cloud computing. Financial institutions depend on digital infrastructure to process transactions and maintain operations. Hospitals, communications networks, logistics companies and energy providers all depend on interconnected systems. Artificial intelligence, which is becoming important to both the American economy and national defense, requires enormous amounts of computing capacity and data.

The building may be privately owned, but the consequences of destroying it may extend far beyond the company that operates it.

AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY

The federal government already recognizes that infrastructure can have national-security implications even when it is not owned by the government. Federal law defines critical infrastructure broadly, including physical or virtual systems and assets whose incapacity or destruction could have a debilitating impact on national security, national economic security, public health or safety.

But our national-security strategy has not fully caught up with the technological transformation of the American economy and military. A generation ago, it was relatively easy to understand why a power plant or port could be considered strategically important. Today, the same logic increasingly applies to the infrastructure that makes the digital economy possible. A data center supporting military logistics, financial markets, telecommunications or advanced artificial intelligence may be just as consequential to national security as a physical facility traditionally associated with defense.

AMERICA RUNS ON DATA. IF WE DON’T BUILD THE INFRASTRUCTURE, CHINA WILL

The Trump administration has recognized the importance of data-center infrastructure to the internet, cloud computing, artificial intelligence and America's economic and national security. Congress should build on that recognition by creating a designation for exceptionally important American-owned or American-controlled digital infrastructure.

The designation should be narrow and subject to rigorous requirements. It should not turn every data center into a national-security facility or give private companies a blank check for government protection.

US ADVERSARY TURNS UP THE HEAT ON AMERICA’S AI LEAD WITH AN UNDERESTIMATED EDGE

Companies seeking the designation should have to meet strict standards concerning ownership and control, cybersecurity, physical security, supply-chain integrity, redundancy and cooperation with U.S. national-security agencies. The federal government could then identify the relatively small number of facilities whose destruction or prolonged incapacitation would pose a serious threat to American national or economic security.

American power increasingly depends on infrastructure that is privately operated and, in some cases, located outside our borders.

These could include data centers supporting military operations, financial markets, critical communications, government systems or strategically important artificial intelligence capabilities.

IRAN-LINKED HACKERS SUSPECTED IN UK POWER-PLANT SHUTDOWN AFTER ALLEGED MINNESOTA WATER ATTACK

The designation would not make these facilities American territory. A data center in Bahrain would not become sovereign American territory simply because it was designated a protected strategic asset. But it would establish something equally important, a clear American policy that deliberately attacking certain strategically vital infrastructure carries consequences.

That clarity serves an important purpose: deterrence.

IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC

Congress should establish a range of potential responses that could include sanctions, asset freezes, diplomatic measures, defensive cyber operations and, depending on the circumstances and attribution, additional measures authorized by Congress.

The goal should not be to automatically escalate every attack into a military confrontation. The goal is to make the consequences sufficiently clear that an adversary thinks twice before attacking.

AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD

Artificial intelligence (AI) only raises the stakes. AI is becoming an ever-more important component of intelligence analysis, cybersecurity, logistics, communications, autonomous systems, military planning and economic competition. President Donald Trump's June 2026 National Security Presidential Memorandum on artificial intelligence (AI) recognized this reality by directing the national-security enterprise to accelerate AI adoption and strengthen partnerships with private industry.

A protestor crashed a pro-data center party in Washington, D.C. claiming the technology is "killing the world." (Vince Natale)

But that raises a critical question: What happens if the infrastructure supporting those systems is attacked?

An adversary may not need to destroy an AI system directly. It could target the data center where the computing takes place, disrupt the electricity supplying the facility, compromise the communications infrastructure connecting it to other systems or attack the supply chain supporting its operations.

If America becomes increasingly dependent on artificial intelligence without protecting the infrastructure underneath it, a strategic advantage could quickly become a strategic vulnerability.

Computing capacity is becoming part of national power. Protecting it needs to become part of national defense.

Our adversaries already understand this. Russia has demonstrated its willingness to use cyber operations and attacks against infrastructure as instruments of state power. China has invested heavily in cyber capabilities and studied vulnerabilities created by America's dependence on interconnected systems. Iran has demonstrated its willingness to use cyber and other asymmetric capabilities against American interests.

They understand that attacking the United States does not necessarily require attacking an American military installation.

The federal government could then identify the relatively small number of facilities whose destruction or prolonged incapacitation would pose a serious threat to American national or economic security.

An adversary could disrupt a power grid, interfere with a port, target a telecommunications network, compromise a financial system or attack the computing infrastructure supporting critical services. That is why digital infrastructure can no longer be treated merely as a technology issue. It is a national-security issue.

For generations, the United States has developed military and diplomatic doctrines designed to deter attacks against the country and its interests. The digital age requires us to expand that thinking.

Congress should establish a framework for identifying the digital infrastructure so important to American national security that its intentional destruction would warrant a significant U.S. response. The administration should then work with allies to develop reciprocal protections for strategically important infrastructure located overseas.

Companies operating designated facilities should also be expected to meet high standards for cybersecurity, physical security, redundancy and resilience. Protection must come with responsibility.

Deterrence does not require eliminating every threat. It requires making the cost of an attack sufficiently clear that an adversary decides the risk is not worth taking.

The United States cannot defend 21st-century power with a 20th-century understanding of national security.

Our borders still matter, and our military installations, ships and aircraft remain essential to national defense. But so do the servers, networks, data centers and computing systems that allow those traditional instruments of power, and increasingly, our entire economy, to function.

The next major attack on American interests may not begin with troops crossing a border or missiles striking a military installation. It could begin with the loss of computing capacity, the disruption of a communications network or the failure of a system most Americans have never heard of but millions depend upon.

Iran has provided a warning about what that future could look like.

The battlefield is expanding beyond traditional military targets and physical borders. America's national-security strategy must expand with it.

The border of the next war may not be on a map. It may be the infrastructure that keeps America running.

Kate Monroe is a Marine Corps veteran, CEO of Vetcomm and author of "The Race to Save America."

articles.title: Head of Jewish Greens says she may leave party over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
articles.excerpt:
Vivien Lichtenstein says she believes motion is unhelpful as anger grows over Zack Polanski’s absence for vote

The head of the Jewish Greens has said she may leave the party after it voted to adopt a...
articles.body_text:
Vivien Lichtenstein says she believes motion is unhelpful as anger grows over Zack Polanski’s absence for vote

The head of the Jewish Greens has said she may leave the party after it voted to adopt a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.

Vivien Lichtenstein said that while opinion among Jewish members of the party was split on the motion passed at its annual conference in Brighton on Sunday, she said she believed it was unhelpful and it was “possible” she might quit.

It comes as anger grows among some in the party about the decision of Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, to miss the vote and to encourage supporters to do the same so they could instead campaign for him in Holborn and St Pancras before the parliamentary byelection for the seat next week.

Polanski sought to have the conference postponed so the party could focus on his efforts to win Keir Starmer’s former seat. When the Greens’ executive committee refused this, the party contacted members, encouraging them to get refunds on their conference tickets to campaign.

Sunday’s binding policy motion was passed by 1,022 votes to 813, and some Greens say more effort by Polanski could have stopped it.

One long-standing member said: “There’s so much anger at his disinterest in such a critical issue. You can’t run a party on vibes alone.”

The motion was opposed by four of the Greens’ five MPs, and is expected to face a legal challenge under equality laws. Polanski did not take a side but justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Lichtenstein condemned the motion: “I don’t think it’s helpful, and it doesn’t make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians.”

Asked if she would remain in the party, she said: “I haven’t decided yet. Certainly it’s quite possible that I will leave the party, and I’m giving it a little time, and to talk with colleagues.”

The motion says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.

Some Jewish Greens have expressed concern that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues. Supporters of the motion, which was led by a group called Greens for Palestine, have said this would not happen.

Asked about this issue, Lichtenstein said she was less worried about being personally targeted than about the potential impact on organisations. She said: “I’m not concerned about people accusing me of supporting Israel’s right to exist, and therefore, I’m a racist, which of course is not the case. I’m just concerned that this is a very bad motion …

“What concerns me is that the party might accuse UK organisations, Jewish organisations, and also Israeli-Jewish and joint Arab-Jewish organisations, of being Zionist and therefore racist. I support an awful lot of those sorts of organisations that are working against the occupation, and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians.”

The idea of calling for a single Palestinian state was not an issue for all Jewish Greens, Lichtenstein said, but party policy had been that it should be “up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future, one state or two”.

The chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, described the motion as “poisonous antisemitism” and a “threat to British Jews and to Britain”.

He said he was “appalled” by the motion, claiming the Green party had resurrected a “discredited and dangerous slander” first promoted by the Soviet Union.

“All decent people will see this for what it is: poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain,” he said.

Israel barred Polanski from entering the country in retaliation for the motion, which the Israeli foreign ministry said “constitute[d] a clear antisemitic text”.

It is understood some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.

Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success. “I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.

articles.title: LEE CARTER: Polls say Democrats could swamp Republicans. As a pollster, I have a question
articles.excerpt:
Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., discusses U.S. job growth under the Trump administration and Democrats’ affordability messaging ahead of the 2026 midterm elections on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

At this rate, ...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., discusses U.S. job growth under the Trump administration and Democrats’ affordability messaging ahead of the 2026 midterm elections on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

At this rate, Democrats may want to stop ordering yard signs and start ordering life jackets.

REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.

President Donald Trump speaks on inflation at Mount Airy Casino Resort in Mount Pocono, Penn., on Tuesday, Dec. 9, 2025. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The polls are very good for Democrats right now. The latest Fox News Power Rankings has Democrats ahead by 11 points among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot. Reuters/Ipsos has them ahead by among registered voters.

LEE CARTER: I STUDY POLLING. DEMOCRATS ARE GAMBLING ON ANTI-TRUMP VOTES, NOT IDEAS

President Donald Trump’s approval rating is struggling. Voters are miserable about prices. Democrats have an enthusiasm advantage.

If you’re a Democrat, there is a lot to like.

If you’re a Republican, maybe skip ahead a few paragraphs.

But I’m a pollster. And when everyone starts looking at the same numbers and reaching the same conclusion, I get a little itchy.

The question is whether we’re asking them to tell us more than they actually can.

The polls are telling us pretty clearly that a lot of Americans are unhappy with Trump.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: VOTERS SAY THEY’RE IN ECONOMIC PAIN, BUT WILL DEMOCRATS GAIN?

What I don’t think they’ve answered yet is whether those same Americans believe in the alternative.

But I’m a pollster. And when everyone starts looking at the same numbers and reaching the same conclusion, I get a little itchy.

100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE

In 2018, Democrats had something wonderfully simple – Healthcare. Not a framework. Not a 14-point plan. Not a word tested in a focus group until everyone in the room agreed it was "accessible." A cause.

Republicans had tried to repeal Obamacare. Voters worried about losing coverage and protections for pre-existing conditions.

You could explain the stakes in about eight seconds.

More importantly, you could finish the sentence:

Former Vice President Kamala Harris joins Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a roundtable discussion at Birth Detroit on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (David Guralnick/Pool/Getty Images)

And it did. Healthcare was the most important issue for more voters than any other issue in polling leading into the 2018 midterms.

MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE

People who charge $24 for a chopped salad are presumably for affordability.

And voters are absolutely furious about prices.

So, the problem isn’t whether voters care about affordability.

The question is: What does affordability mean Democrats are actually going to do?

Because affordability describes the problem beautifully.

So, what fills in the blank in 2026? Well, Democrats have a word. Affordability. And it is having quite a year.

It doesn’t necessarily describe the solution.

REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS

That’s where, to me, the numbers get interesting. Pew asked Americans which party’s economic policies they agreed with more.

Remember the environment we’re talking about.

Only 24% rated the economy good or excellent. Six in 10 said Trump’s economic policies had made economic conditions worse.

The economy is front and center. Trump is struggling. Democrats are leading the congressional ballot.

Jimmy Kimmel revealed that his interview with James Talarico would only air on YouTube, citing FCC threats during "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" on Sept. 9, 2026. (Randy Holmes/Disney via Getty Images; Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

One point. Not even the margin of error. That’s the number I can’t stop thinking about.

Because Democrats may be winning the referendum on Trump without yet winning the argument for themselves.

And those are two very different victories.

This is where I think we may be getting ahead of ourselves.

A voter can be unhappy with Trump without falling madly in love with Democrats.

These are not mutually exclusive positions.

In fact, judging by Americans’ views of politics generally, they may be the national consensus.

You can think Republicans have failed on prices without believing Democrats know how to fix them.

You can prefer a Democrat when a pollster calls in September and still not be particularly motivated to vote in November.

You can desperately want change and remain profoundly unconvinced by your available choices.

That’s why I’m not dismissing today’s Democratic polling advantage.

The economy is front and center. Trump is struggling. Democrats are leading the congressional ballot. And yet, on economic policy: Democrats: 37%. Republicans: 36%.

Because causes get people out of the house.

Democrats also have the small matter of deciding what they believe

There isn’t exactly one Democratic Party right now.

There is a progressive Democratic Party talking about corporate power, housing and fundamental economic change.

There is a center-left Democratic Party talking about competence, stability and lowering costs.

There are Democrats trying to win back Trump voters.

Democrats trying to rebuild the Obama coalition.

Democrats trying to create a new coalition altogether.

I’m less certain they would all finish the sentence the same way.

And voters don’t only need to know what you’re against.

Eventually, they want to know where you’re taking them.

And what on earth do Republicans do with that?

This is where Republicans might want to resist a favorite Washington pastime: explaining to voters why voters are wrong.

If people say groceries are too expensive, telling them the economy is actually terrific is unlikely to make the eggs cheaper.

If they say they’re exhausted by chaos, producing more chaos seems an unusual voter-retention strategy.

And if they say affordability is their biggest concern, changing the subject may work for a news cycle. It doesn’t change the grocery bill.

Vice President J.D. Vance (C), accompanied by (L-R) Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Deputy Administrator & Chief Operating Officer Kimberly Brandt, Administrator for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz, Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, and Health and Human Services Deputy Secretary nominee Chris Klomp, speaks during a news conference on fraud at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building on Sept. 22, 2026, in Washington, DC. Vance announced a federal crackdown on Affordable Care Act fraud, removing over 750,000 allegedly ineligible enrollments and banning hundreds of suspect brokers to save taxpayers an estimated $2.2 billion. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Voters haven’t completely abandoned Republican policies.

Pew found the parties essentially tied on economic policy. Republicans still had an advantage on immigration and a much larger advantage on crime.

So, this isn’t necessarily an electorate saying:

We have embraced the Democratic worldview.

We don’t particularly like what you’re doing with the keys.

They can all say affordability. I’m less certain they would all finish the sentence the same way. And voters don’t only need to know what you’re against. Eventually, they want to know where you’re taking them.

Democrats have to turn dissatisfaction into belief.

Republicans have to convince voters that the things they elected them to do are actually making their lives better if they get more time.

For Democrats, it’s the gap between rejection and conversion.

For Republicans, it’s the gap between policy and lived experience.

And neither one gets across that gap by shouting affordability more loudly.

Voters already know things cost too much.

They don’t need another politician to identify the problem.

They need some reason to believe somebody can actually solve it.

I’m a pollster, so I want to be very clear:

When poll after poll shows Democrats ahead, that’s meaningful.

When Trump’s approval falls, that’s meaningful.

When voters repeatedly say affordability is their biggest concern, that’s meaningful.

A poll is doing its job when it tells us where voters are today.

Where we get into trouble is when we turn a snapshot into a screenplay and start writing the ending.

Michigan and Wisconsin gave us a useful reminder of that this summer.

The lesson wasn’t that polling is broken.

For Democrats, it’s the gap between rejection and conversion. For Republicans, it’s the gap between policy and lived experience. And neither one gets across that gap by shouting affordability more loudly.

And enthusiasm can sometimes make one group much easier to see than another.

Intensity isn’t prevalence. And prevalence isn’t turnout.

It’s an argument against getting cocky about it.

The current political environment gives Democrats plenty of reasons for optimism.

Affordability could become the 2026 version of healthcare.

Opposition to Trump could itself become the motivating cause.

Democrats could spend the remaining weeks turning "affordability" from a word into an argument voters understand and believe.

But that’s different from saying the outcome is inevitable.

What strikes me most about voters right now isn’t enthusiasm.

Members of Congress begin to arrive in the House Chamber before US President Donald Trump delivers the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on February 24, 2026. (ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS / AFP via Getty Images)

They’re tired of paying too much for everything.

They may even be tired of being asked how tired they are.

And volatile electorates have a nasty habit of embarrassing people who think they’ve figured them out.

So yes, Democrats should be happy about the polls.

Republicans should be worried about them.

But neither party should mistake unhappiness for allegiance.

The question that will decide this election isn’t simply whether Americans are disappointed in Donald Trump.

It’s whether Democrats can give those voters something affirmative to believe in.

Democrats could spend the remaining weeks turning "affordability" from a word into an argument voters understand and believe. But that’s different from saying the outcome is inevitable.

And whether Republicans can give them something affirmative to choose.

One was a cause. The other is still a word. For now.

Lee Hartley Carter is a communications strategist and public opinion expert. She's the founder and CEO of Carter Intelligence Group and author of "Persuasion: Convincing Others When Facts Don't Seem to Matter" (TarcherPerigee, September 3, 2019). Follow her on X on @lh_carter.
