A co-host, meteorologist Rachel Duensing, tried to get her to pump the brakes on the oversharing about Brind’Amour. It evidently worked on air, but she still felt the need to share the clip on social media until it was disabled or deleted.

You live and you learn. I'm not going to go after her for allowing her heart to take her too deep into the romantic waters. I think if she had to do it again, she'd dial it back a little and that's good enough for me.

Getting lost in tarps off celebrations, the likes of which Rod Brind'Amour was involved in, could happen to anyone.

articles.title: France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called
articles.excerpt:
France plans to fully or partially close up to 500 schools on Monday amid a series of student protests that have become increasingly violent.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced the precauti...
articles.body_text:
France plans to fully or partially close up to 500 schools on Monday amid a series of student protests that have become increasingly violent.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced the precautionary measures on Sunday as part of a bid for a “partial, progressive return to lessons”. However, after a weekend lull, student protestors announced they plan to resume demonstrations – launched last month over complaints regarding class sizes, lack of teachers, and other complaints – early in the week.

Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some “400-500” high schools as the security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the minister said. He added that 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the protests.

Geffray said the closures were a security precaution. Protest organisers have called for a return to large-scale demonstrations on Tuesday, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from President Emmanuel Macron’s government.

At least 170 students and 78 educational personnel have been injured since the student demos first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September, according to Geffray.

The Ministry of National Education reported that at least 400 of the 3,700 high schools in France were closed on Friday, while 560 faced protests or disruptions.

The number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday, Geffray said.

Teachers and students first mobilised at a high school in a Paris suburb on 17 September over a lack of teaching staff, excessive school-day hours and other grievances. The protests have since spread nationwide, resulting in class strikes, blockades and demonstrations.

According to the interior minister, more than 5,000 people have been arrested in the last week; 85 percent of them minors.

Critics have criticised “disproportionate” police violence in response to the demonstrations. Rights group Amnesty International said the student protestors “must be listened to, not repressed”.

In an interview on French public radio, Geffray claimed far-left activists “infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves and engaged in extreme violence.”

The Milwaukee Brewers got an out in despite the ball hitting the roof in the ninth inning against the San Diego Padres.

If there's one thing the Major League Baseball postseason always delivers, it's drama. And Saturday night's game between the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers certainly had more than its fair share.

The Brewers entered the game and the series as big favorites, thanks in large part to likely NL Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski starting game one. Misiorowski has been nearly unhittable this season, with a minuscule 1.80 ERA, just 96 hits allowed all season, and 252 strikeouts in 174.2 innings. But the Padres have been baseball's hottest team down the stretch, and were able to force him out after pushing across two runs in just four innings.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But the Brewers battled back, tying the game on a Jackson Chourio homer and taking the lead late on another from William Contreras. The Padres missed an opportunity in the top of the 8th, but started the 9th with the heart of their lineup facing closer Trevor Megill. Dustin Harris singled to lead off the ninth, Manny Machado struck out, and Ty France launched what's now become one of the most controversial fly balls in recent postseason history.

BREWERS TAKE GAME 1 OF NLDS AFTER A CONTROVERSIAL CALL ON SURE-FIRE HOME RUN BALL THAT HIT THE STADIUM ROOF

Milwaukee Brewers hard-throwing righty and presumptive NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski got his first postseason start in Game 1 of the NLDS against the San Diego Padres. (Photo by Rob Tringali/MLB Photos via Getty Images)

While it looked at first glance like a potential go-ahead home run, or might fly harmlessly foul, France hit the ball so high it banged off the roof support system at American Family Field and fell into the field of play just onto the warning track in left field, where Jackson Chourio caught it for an out.

Several minutes of discussion followed, with the umpires ruling on the field that it was, in fact, a fair ball and effectively a fly ball out. Many fans, and some of the players, were clearly confused, assuming that a ball hitting the roof would become immediately "dead" and the play restarted.

By rule though, there's no question that the umpires made the correct call. Major League Baseball's ground rule page, specifically covering American Family Field, covers this exact situation. If the "Batted ball strikes roof, roof truss, roof cable, or any cabling over fair territory," the rule states, it's considered "In Play."

"If caught by fielder," it continues, "batter is out, and runners advance at own risk."

That's exactly what was determined on the field, and what the replay review confirmed. The ball was in fair territory when it hit the roof, it fell down to the field of play where it was caught by an outfielder, and the hitter is out. Controversy over, right?

Padres first baseman Ty France reacts after his almost certain home run ricocheted off the stadium's roof and was caught for an out. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images)

Many fans, obviously most notably Padres fans, are convinced that the ball would have been a home run had it not hit the roof. France himself said as much after the game in the clubhouse. "You would think with all the technology we have now we’d be able to make a clear call on that," France said. "There should be something put in place right there. That shouldn’t be an out. … We’ve got ball tracking. We’ve got exit velo. We’ve got projected distances. We have all that stuff."

And that's where the second part of the controversy has continued, and even grown. Had the ball not hit the roof, would it have been a game, and potentially series, changing home run?

France is right; we do have ball tracking, exit velocity and projected distances, thanks to the league's Statcast operation. And those metrics all but confirmed one thing: that was not going to be a home run.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Statcast measured France's fly ball at 105.3mph exit velocity at a whopping 49 degree launch angle. The projected distance? 325 feet. The wall in Milwaukee? Well, it's hard to know exactly where the ball would have come down if unobstructed, but the shortest dimension is 342 feet directly at the foul pole. Had the ball been more towards left center, it's even further.

There's more to it than that. Statcast predicted "expected" batting average, essentially how often balls hit with those exact characteristics become hits, was .050. Balls hit 105.3mph at 49 degrees are outs 99.5% of the time. They're also home runs in just one stadium: Daikin Park in Houston, thanks to the short porch with the Crawford Boxes.

Thanks to Statcast, we can compare similarly hit baseballs with that exact launch angle and see the results. Here's the list from 2026:

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Expanding the search to 2024 and 2025, there were a number of other balls that met these exact characteristics. Of the 15 batted ball events, including 2026, 14 were outs, with one double from Aaron Judge in 2024. The furthest a batted ball traveled with those exact numbers was 337 feet, a fly ball from Cody Bellinger in April 2025.

San Diego Padres' Ty France watches his ball hit a cable near the roof of American Family Field during the ninth inning of Game 1 of a National League Division Series on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Chris Carlson)

There are different outcomes because of weather conditions, the exact backspin of the ball, and many other variables. But with the exact measurements available to us, not a single ball hit with that velocity and launch angle traveled far enough to cover the left field wall at American Family Field, even if it were directly down the line.

France, though, was convinced it was "going out."

"I guess the biggest question was whether it was going to stay fair or foul," he said. "I thought I backspun it and thought it was going to stay fair. Knew it was going out."

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Except we've seen, countless times, players look as though they expect a ball to fly for a homer, only to die on the warning track. Players aren't reliable narrators when it comes to judging distance. Data is. And the data shows France's fly ball wouldn't have cleared the fence.

Fluky and bizarre and open to endless debate? Yes. Postseason robbery? No.

articles.title: Majority Leader Thune warns Chuck Schumer 'lives in fear' of socialists taking over Democratic Party
articles.excerpt:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune says the GOP’s legislative agenda is giving people more money in their pockets on ‘My View with Lara Trump.’

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Senate Minority L...
articles.body_text:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune says the GOP’s legislative agenda is giving people more money in their pockets on ‘My View with Lara Trump.’

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer "lives in fear" of the Democratic Party's far-left wing Saturday on "My View with Lara Trump," arguing the longtime New York lawmaker has increasingly deferred to progressives as Republicans and Democrats head into the final stretch before the midterm elections.

"I think he lives in fear of that every day. I really do," Thune, R-S.D., said when asked whether he thinks Schumer is concerned with being overtaken by "socialists."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he thinks Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., "lives in fear" of being overtaken by the Democratic Party's far-left flank. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon; AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

"I look at the way that the leaders in the Senate now act, and he voted once to open up the government when they were in the process of shutting it down the first time, and it just got blown up by the far left. And ever since then, I mean, it's kind of whatever they want. They defer to that far-left base."

Thune made the remarks while discussing what he characterized as Democratic pushback in the Senate, arguing Republicans have been unable to advance several pieces of legislation that are traditionally supported by both parties, like military funding.

TED CRUZ NAMES ‘MOST POWERFUL DEMOCRAT’ AS HE WARNS SOCIALIST RISE HAS PARALYZED BIPARTISANSHIP

"We have a saying in my office that if you don't get national security right, the rest is conversation. You've got to protect the country. And so funding our military, the defense authorization bill, as I mentioned earlier — the Democrats blocked us from even getting on it on the floor. Historically, that's been bipartisan," Thune said.

He also emphasized the importance of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which he said is "critical to our intelligence community."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat from New York, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 11, 2025. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Those are the kinds of things that keep me up at night. I think, to me, it's always about keeping this country safe and secure. Since that problem is kind of now solved, people are like, 'OK, what have you done for me lately?' And obviously, you know, we've got more to do."

"But the trajectory that we are on as a country, when it comes to economic policy, national security, the border, all these issues, we are headed in the right direction," he added.

SENATE DEMS DRAW RARE LINE AGAINST MUST-PASS PENTAGON BILL

The South Dakota senator outlined Republicans' legislative priorities should the GOP retain control of Congress in November, which included military funding, judicial nominations, permitting reform and more.

"If we can maintain the majorities in the House and the Senate, the sky's the limit," he said.

Thune's remarks follow several prominent victories for Democratic socialist candidates, including recent wins in high-profile primary elections across state and local levels. In New York City, Darializa Avila Chevalier, the 32-year-old community organizer backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, narrowly topped incumbent Democrat Adriano Espaillat, the 71-year-old Congressional Hispanic Caucus chair and the first Dominican American elected to the U.S. House.

Mamdani-endorsed state Assembly member Claire Valdez, who won her primary in June in New York's 7th District, emphasized in her victory speech that "we haven't just won an election. We have declared that this movement is durable — that it is growing, and that it will not stop until working people are no longer asked to just build the table, no longer just offered a seat at the table, but will run the table."

While progressive figures continue to push the party leftward, Schumer has trod carefully, seeking to keep the party unified under a "big tent" strategy. Over the summer, he dodged a question from Fox News about whether the Democratic Socialists of America's platform has a place in the Democratic Party.

"[The] bottom line is Democrats from one end of the spectrum to the other are going to be working to defeat Trump, to bring down costs, to go after his corruption and to end the chaos," Schumer replied at a leadership news conference.

The Senate minority leader did not elaborate on whether he agreed with the DSA’s call to abolish the Senate.

Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer for comment but did not immediately hear back.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser, Adam Pack and Kelly Phares contributed to this report.

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

articles.title: Pro-Imran Khan mass rally launched after Pakistan government talks fail
articles.excerpt:
Supporters of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan have set off on a protest march from the country’s northwest after talks with the government to call off the demonstration failed.

More...
articles.body_text:
Supporters of jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan have set off on a protest march from the country’s northwest after talks with the government to call off the demonstration failed.

More than 5,000 were reported to have begun the rally on Sunday. The march, planned by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed until October 4 to allow talks between the government and the PTI leadership to take place.

However, two rounds of talks over the weekend failed to break the deadlock, and the PTI decided to carry out its plan, which is the latest attempt to pressure the government into releasing Khan, the country’s most popular political figure according to polls, who has been behind bars since August 2023 following a series of convictions that his party calls politically motivated.

All but one of the convictions against the former PM have since been suspended or overturned on appeal.

Videos posted on the PTI’s official social media showed supporters joining the march in different areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which is ruled by the party, and setting off in convoys.

Sohail Afridi, the region’s chief minister, had earlier posted on social media that the demonstration in support of Khan would go ahead.

He said the march will make its way to Khairabad, 80 kilometres (50 miles) west of Islamabad, by Thursday, where the plan for the “next phase” will be announced.

The government has been preparing for weeks for the arrival of PTI demonstrators in Islamabad. It has erected barriers using shipping containers to block main access routes to the capital.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi confirmed earlier on Sunday that the talks between the two sides had failed.  He accused Afridi of “sabotaging” the negotiations, and added that the government would not allow the PTI to “create a disturbance”.

He also cited an Islamabad High Court order from September 14, ruling that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”.

“If they violate the orders, whether they are workers or politicians, whether they are protesting within KP or outside KP, we will pursue them one by one. This time, we want to ensure that these repeated episodes of creating disturbance in Islamabad come to an end,” Naqvi said.

Concerns about the 73-year-old Khan’s health, in particular the condition of his right eye that has required months of specialist treatment, have prompted the PTI’s campaign for his release.

The party has also called for the release of Khan’s three sisters, whose arrests last month further heightened tensions.

James Dorsey, a fellow at the National University of Singapore, said Khan was “essentially a populist leader” with “a genuine popular movement that had broad popular support”.

That is behind the “determination by the government to prevent [the protesters] from entering Islamabad,” he told the AFP news agency.

Given Pakistan’s security concerns, particularly following its unresolved February 2026 conflict with Afghanistan, Islamabad wants to avoid escalation in the face of the protests, he added.

“It’s a problem for the government, but I don’t think it’s an existential threat,” he said.

articles.title: Odell Beckham Jr laments his short-lived return to the New York Giants: 'I should have known better'
articles.excerpt: Ex-NFL wide receiver Chad Ochocinco couldn't be happier for Odell Beckham Jr. making the New York Giants' 53-man roster for the 2026 NFL season. He believes he could make an impact, but fans shouldn't...
articles.body_text:
Ex-NFL wide receiver Chad Ochocinco couldn't be happier for Odell Beckham Jr. making the New York Giants' 53-man roster for the 2026 NFL season. He believes he could make an impact, but fans shouldn't expect the old Giants Beckham.

It was nice while it lasted for Odell Beckham's fateful return to the New York Giants. When the club released him last week, his silence suggested he was appreciative of the opportunity and the time that the reunion lasted.

Then Beckham took to a fan's Instagram account on Saturday and the narrative changed completely.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

EX-NFL STAR BELIEVES ODELL BECKHAM JR 'STILL BETTER THAN MOST OF THE RECEIVERS' IN NFL AS HE RETURNS TO GIANTS

Yes, welcome to 2026 when fans can post their complaints about an NFL franchise's coach, general manager and business decisions, and a disgruntled former player can join the conversation and agree.

Beckham is apparently agreeing with the premise that the Giants used him, and paid minimally for it in return. That was surprising.

"I'm super smart!!!! But I didn't see this one, my brotha," Beckham complained in his reply to the post. "They got me!!!"

New York Giants wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. celebrates during a game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on Aug. 28, 2026, in East Rutherford, N.J. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"They won on top of the money u talkin [about], I made them. I came in HUMBLY took vet min then EARNED my spot [and] didn’t say nothing bout no $$$ which I [know] make for everybody

"Ima tell u this ima grown man and this [sh-t] didn’t hurt me but it did when they cut me like that cause part of me is like I shoulda known better."

GIANTS WORKING OUT MULTIPLE RECEIVERS INCLUDING ODELL BECKHAM JR, WHILE EAGLES LOOK TO TRADE AJ BROWN

Beckham signed a one-year veterans salary benefit deal with the Giants. That meant the team didn't have to pay him the veteran minimum and there was no guaranteed money.

Sep 30, 2018; East Rutherford, NJ, USA; New York Giants wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. (13) reacts during the third quarter against the New Orleans Saints at MetLife Stadium. (Brad Penner-USA TODAY Sports)

And it was a fun story for a minute. Beckham originally played for the Giants from 2014-18 and was something of a prince in the city for a time.

His return was seen as a warm homecoming, with Beckham saying he never wanted to leave and was happy to be back. He didn't even demand his own number back.

But the return was more interesting in the press than on the field because Beckham, 33, was active for three games but caught zero passes after being targeted just once.

Beckham was released on Sept. 29. And then the sting of the release hit days later.

"Now let me [tell] u the [real] deal truth [that] hurt my heart to the core is [coming] home and seeing my son and how happy he was with no idea of what happened and talkin' [about] my job [and] jersey number 13 broke me [the f–k] down," Beckham wrote.

Head coach John Harbaugh of the New York Giants reacts during the second quarter of a game against the Dallas Cowboys at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 13, 2026, in East Rutherford, N.J. (Getty Images)

Beckham is accusing the Giants of giving him "the run along," and is upset by that because it meant he couldn't pursue opportunities on other teams through training camp, the preseason, and most of September.

"[I don't know] why they even gave me the run along. I [could have] really been playing this year somewhere and making [an] impact and I mean that from a person whose humbled by God and life."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

One supposes Beckham feels better unburdening himself by making public all that's on his mind.

New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh speaks to the media after being introduced during a news conference at the teams NFL football training facility Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026, in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (AP Photo/Adam Hunger)

But this might not be the wise move. That's because releasing a player is as temporary as signing him.

The Giants could easily consider a Beckham return if circumstances, such as injuries, were to befall their receivers. But now Beckham has openly criticized the team and that could be a problem.

Most teams, you see, don't want to re-sign players that have been publicly critical of them.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Bengals' Ja'Marr Chase suffers concussion after getting his facemask pulled and taking huge hit

The Cincinnati Bengals’ offense ...
articles.body_text:
Julian Edelman gives Joe Burrow a list of names from the Bengals organization to play word association with including Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, and Dexter Lawrence.

The Cincinnati Bengals’ offense took a huge hit on Sunday against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Putting quarterback Joe Burrow's first-half interception to the side for a second, the team really couldn’t afford to lose anyone on the offense. Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Mike Gesicki are just some of the integral parts of what makes Cincinnati’s offense run.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Jarrian Jones gets a face mask penalty against Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'marr Chase during an NFL game in Cincinnati on Oct. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Joshua A. Bickel)

When a play like the one that happened to Chase comes, Bengals fans have to have had a pit in their stomachs.

Chase caught a routine pass on the left side of the field in the second quarter. He tried to make a move around Jaguars cornerback Jarrian Jones. Instead, Jones grabbed a handful of Chase’s facemask, ripping it around the star wide receiver’s head. Chase shook off Jones’ grip but he took a huge hit from linebacker Ventrell Miller. Jones was penalized for grabbing the facemask.

Chase went down and that would be the last bit of action he would see.

The Bengals announced that Chase was being evaluated for a concussion and was questionable to return. The team said at the start of the second half that Chase would miss the remainder of the game.

Jacksonville Jaguars cornerback Travis Hunter tackles Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'marr Chase during an NFL game in Cincinnati on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Joshua A. Bickel)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Cincinnati was only able to muster three points against the Jaguars in the first half, which may speak more to Jacksonville’s relentless defense to start the 2026 season than Cincinnati’s offense. Regardless, Chase’s injury is a huge hole in the offense – that part doesn’t really need to be said.

Burrow found Gesicki for a touchdown on the Bengals’ first drive of the second half as they looked to get back in the game.

Chase, a five-time Pro Bowler, got back into form over the last two weeks. He had 16 catches for 173 yards and three touchdowns in the last two games.

Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'marr Chase reacts after scoring a touchdown during the first half of an NFL football game against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Pittsburgh on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar)

Cincinnati was 2-1 entering Week 4 against Jacksonville.

articles.title: Jason Kelce calls the Commanders the 'Redskins' during game, immediately apologizes so as to not get canceled
articles.excerpt: Craig Carton is calling out Amazon and Taylor Rooks for the interview they conducted with controversial Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson during Thursday Night Football, with Carton wishing ...
articles.body_text:
Craig Carton is calling out Amazon and Taylor Rooks for the interview they conducted with controversial Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson during Thursday Night Football, with Carton wishing they asked the questions people wanted answers too

Jason Kelce acted as if he committed an unpardonable broadcasting sin Sunday afternoon while serving as a booth analyst for NFL Network during the Washington Commanders game against the Indianapolis Colts.

He called the team in burgundy and gold the Washington Redskins.

Former player Jason Kelce reacts prior to the game between the Washington Commanders and the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium. The game took place in Kansas City, Missouri, on Oct. 27, 2025. (Jamie Squire/Getty Images)

CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL BATTLES NEWSOM'S STATE LAW ORDERING IT TO CHANGE 'INDIANS' MASCOT

This is actually nothing if you're a normal person who is aware the Commanders were the Redskins for decades until that name got canceled by an outcry to mostly liberal voices claiming "Redskins" is a racist insult.

(Native Americans have both agreed and vehemently disagreed the term is racist – it mostly depends on what group with an agenda one asks).

Anyway, back to Kelce. Look, he's still trying to settle into his broadcasting role three years after retiring from the Philadelphia Eagles.

He was a 13-year NFL center of the highest caliber, so he's outstanding at explaining offensive line play.

Former NFL player and ESPN commentator Jason Kelce is on the sidelines during the game between the Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, on Nov. 4, 2024. (Denny Medley/Imagn Images)

This booth analyst gig is mostly new for Kelce and he got all fired up explaining the Commanders' play in the secondary.

"Washington's secondary has been great on third down," Kelce said under replays of plays by the unit. "...When you're in man to man coverage, it just takes one missed tackle, and that can turn into a huge play.

"The Redskins right now are doing a great job of not only staying tight, but making the play when the ball is in the receiver's hand and keeping it short of the sticks."

Play-by-play announcer Dave Pasch immediately chimed in, "Commanders. You did it."

ESPN Monday Night Football broadcaster Jason Kelce is on the set before a game between the Philadelphia Eagles and Atlanta Falcons at Lincoln Financial Field on Sept. 16, 2024, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Eric Hartline/Imagn Images)

"You said Redskins," Pasch said, repeating that nickname that is both beloved and blackballed.

"Oh, my gosh!" Kelce exclaimed. "I almost made it out."

The three men in the booth that included Hall of Fame quarterback Kurt Warner as another analyst, apparently talked about the possibility of inadvertently using the Redskins name on air before the game.

"Yeah, the three of us had a little gentleman's bet who would be first," Pasch said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Washington Redskins great Sonny Jurgensen is introduced prior to game action against the San Diego Chargers. The introduction took place at FedEx Field in Landover, Maryland, on Nov. 3, 2013. (Jonathan Newton/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

And all this shows the utter stupidity of the whole name change thing.

If one were to take a poll of whether the Redskins should continue to be called the Redskins, as they were in Washington since 1937 to 2020, it is likely a large portion of respondents would definitely want the traditional nickname to return.

And, yes, there are people who would still want the old nickname banished to the memory of what they believe was a racist time. Washington owner Josh Harris is apparently in this group, and he gets the final call.

But one simply cannot erase history – although some people try.

The Redskins were beloved in Washington. Kelce played against them during nine of his 13 seasons with that team.

Scott Turner is seen in Redskins red on the field in 1995 (Joseph Patronite/Getty Images)

TAYLOR HEINICKE RETIRES FROM THE NFL WITH A FAREWELL SALUTE TO THE WASHINGTON REDSKINS

Many players who wore the Indian head helmet logo inspired by Blackfeet Chief John Two Guns White Calf and heard the, "Hail to the Redskins," fight song echo in their ears during home games, continue to hold allegiance to the Redskins nickname.

The NFL Network booth, led by Pasch's lighthearted approach to this flub, struck the right tone.

Liberals may not like it. But Diron Talbert, Dave Butz, Darryl Grant and Jonathan Allen aren't coming after you.

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest
articles.excerpt:
Young people have been protesting against large-scale changes to voter rolls by the Election Commission

Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during stre...
articles.body_text:
Young people have been protesting against large-scale changes to voter rolls by the Election Commission

Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.

The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.

In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.

The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.

Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.

The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this".

"Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.

She said the police were resorting to "brutality".

The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists.

"Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement.

Demonstrators scuffle with police during a protest in New Delhi over the alleged assault

The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.

But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.

The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement.

The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms.

The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express, external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.

The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.

The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously.

But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation.

India's 'cockroach' protesters are back - this time asking poll chief to resign

Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again

articles.title: Neighborhood backlash collides with America's tech arms race — but is this the plan to fix it?
articles.excerpt:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., says Washington needs a new playbook to win community buy-in as the US races China for technological dominance

A national security push to expand the infrastructure beh...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., says Washington needs a new playbook to win community buy-in as the US races China for technological dominance

A national security push to expand the infrastructure behind America's technological ambitions is running into resistance from the communities being asked to host it, pitting Washington's race to stay ahead of China against mounting local backlash.

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., who represents America’s "Data Center Alley," warns that backlash could obstruct the very buildout Washington considers a national priority unless Congress steps in — arguing that community buy-in is necessary to keep expansion moving.

"The communities are being steamrolled by the industry," Subramanyam told Fox News Digital. "They’re not feeling like anyone’s listening to them."

Subramanyam is pitching a four-part federal plan aimed at breaking what he sees as a false choice between unchecked development and outright moratoriums. The proposal addresses siting, power costs, energy and water measurement, and security for the facilities and surrounding communities.

TRUMP’S DATA CENTER PUSH FRACTURES CONGRESS AS LOCAL ANGER EXPLODES: 'GRASPING AT STRAWS'

Ashburn, Virginia, is the center of Data Center Alley. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"If you are concerned about a race with China, when it comes to building data centers and AI, you should want to work with us on a plan to get community buy-in for where to build data centers," Subramanyam said.

His Fair Share Act would push states to require large power users to cover more of the infrastructure costs needed to serve them, according to the plan.

HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF

An Amazon Web Services data center in Stone Ridge, Virginia, on July 28, 2024. (Nathan Howard/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"At the federal level, if we say that we're going to take away some of your federal funding if you do this, then it will be a no-brainer," he said, arguing data centers should "pay their fair share for the infrastructure that needs to be built because of them."

The tension surfaced again this week as Fox News Digital reported on complaints of noise and encroachment from a massive data center built against an Ashburn cul-de-sac.

Subramanyam said many residents in his district understand the need for the infrastructure but object to how he says its costs and burdens are distributed.

Loudoun County says data center revenue has helped it lower its real-property tax rate, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026, according to the county.

But Subramanyam argued residents must weigh those benefits against costs he says can appear elsewhere, particularly on utility bills.

"What's not OK is feeling like they come in, jack up utility costs and we pay for their power infrastructure," he said, also citing water, air quality and other community concerns.

The industry disputes that data centers are driving higher residential power bills. The Leesburg-based Data Center Coalition has cited a recent analysis by energy consulting firm E3 that found no historical evidence that data centers increased residential electricity costs under existing rate structures.

Fox News Digital reached out to the trade group, which is based in Data Center Alley, for comment on the package.

Subramanyam argues infrastructure with national implications cannot continue developing "ad hoc" under a patchwork of state and local rules.

CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., speaks on the Hill. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

Other pieces of the plan would establish federal standards for siting and measurement and develop protections against security threats, including attacks on critical infrastructure overseas.

"I know that localities do zoning, states do energy policy and other related things, but Congress and the federal government need to get involved," Subramanyam said.

AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Those concerns have also become a focus of state action. Gov. Abigail Spanberger unveiled a September framework aimed at strengthening local control, shifting more infrastructure costs onto major power users and setting new standards for water use and grid reliability.

"In the years before I took office, data centers came to Virginia, and the commonwealth did not have a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians — on their electric bills, their water, their land, their air, or their quality of life," Spanberger told Fox News Digital.

Leaders across the political spectrum, from Spanberger to Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, have crafted plans and emphasized the issue’s importance on multiple fronts.

Just across the Blue Ridge, West Virginia has taken a different approach, creating a microgrid program designed to attract large projects. Critics have raised concerns about limits on local government powers, while proponents have mapped out potential property tax elimination.

Jefferson County stakeholders recently debated the issue with the state's data-economy liaison at a forum in Shepherdstown, where county Commissioner Cara Keys criticized the potential loss of local control while the liaison maintained that project approvals would be handled judiciously, according to WVMetroNews.

"Two things can be true: You can support data centers, and you can be against the guardrails lacking in [the law]," Keys said.

A welcome sign is posted in the grass near the intersection of Lee Highway, Key Bridge and the George Washington Memorial Parkway in Rosslyn, Arlington County, Virginia. (Universal Images Group/Getty Images)

For Subramanyam, the sharply different approaches on either side of the Blue Ridge illustrate the patchwork he says Washington must address before local resistance hardens further.

"The only plan I've seen is either to do nothing or a full moratorium," he said. "And to me, neither of those is a viable option moving forward."

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

articles.title: Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day
articles.excerpt:
Thousands of youth and opposition protesters have rallied for a third day in India demanding the resignation of the country’s election commission chief.

Thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, while o...
articles.body_text:
Thousands of youth and opposition protesters have rallied for a third day in India demanding the resignation of the country’s election commission chief.

Thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, while others gathered for a third day of demonstrations in New Delhi. The protests began on Friday demanding that Election Commission of India (ECI) chief Gyanesh Kumar step down due to reports that he has overseen voter-roll revisions removing millions from electoral lists.

Protesters say the disenfranchisement stands to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the ECI and the BJP have denied the allegations.

Led by opposition leaders Raj Thackeray and Uddhav Thackeray, thousands marched in Mumbai on Sunday, waving Indian flags and calling for Kumar to step down.

In the capital, New Delhi, protesters started gathering in the early evening. As on previous days, some were detained by police as they arrived, according to the Reuters news agency.

Police in the capital have clamped down in a bid to prevent protesters from assembling over the last two days, detaining dozens and taking them away by bus.

Some of the detainees were released later on Friday and Saturday, but police registered cases against some on charges of violating orders banning mass gatherings in the centre of the capital.

“⁠I just want to tell the ruling party this much … We are angry about how you are wielding that power. ⁠It’s the people of this country who should decide who sits in power and who sits in opposition, not the election commission,” Raj Thackeray told the crowd in Mumbai.

The ECI says the voter-roll revision is designed to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls.

Kumar has not publicly responded to the demands for his resignation or commented on the protests, which look set to continue over the coming days, with more rallies planned.

An alliance of India’s opposition parties plans to launch protests to “save democracy” with a march to the election commission office on Tuesday. The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced plans for a major rally in New Delhi on October 10.

“Mumbai is out on the streets again for free and fair elections!” Abhijeet Dipke, chief of the CJP, said in a social media post on Sunday.

“Solidarity with all the protesters,” he added. “All Indians need to come together. It’s now or never!”

Sometimes, being at an Ivy League institution matters.

A quick-thinking lateral, after a brutal false start, helped the Harvard Crimson defeat the Colgate Raiders on Saturday night 20-17.

Ryan Tattersall No. 22 of the Harvard Crimson celebrates his touchdown against the Yale Bulldogs in the first half of the 141st playing of The Game at Yale Bowl in New Haven, Conn., on Nov. 22, 2025. (Getty Images)

The Raiders thought they had a victory wrapped up when quarterback Jake Stearney threw a 13-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver Matt Fogler with 27 seconds left in the game. The Crimson had more than enough time to do something with the football and at least tie the game to force overtime.

Harvard quarterback Charlie Smith moved the ball up the field and gave kicker Francisco Moscoso a chance to tie the game with a long field goal. However, the Crimson special teams committed a false start penalty, causing Harvard to be moved out of field goal range.

Smith had one last snap. He took the ball and fired it downfield to Teigan Pelletier, who was well short of the end zone. Pelletier tried to carry multiple Raiders defenders on his back before he saw Nate Bailey and tossed him the football. Bailey rushed the ball into the end zone as time expired.

Harvard won the game, moving to 3-0 on the year.

College football fans went wild as the clip went viral across social media.

Bailey finished with 16 catches for 197 yards and a touchdown. His receptions mark is the second-most in a single game in Harvard history – five short of Carl Owens and one better than Kyle Juszczyk. Smith finished with 369 passing yards and two touchdown passes.

Stearney was 21-of-39 with 188 passing yards and a touchdown pass. Fogler finished with 12 catches for 138 yards and a touchdown.

articles.title: Yemen's government announces all-out war to reclaim land from Houthis
articles.excerpt:
Soldiers ride in the back of a pick-up truck on a dirt road near Taiz, amid fighting between Yemeni government forces and Houthis

The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announc...
articles.body_text:
Soldiers ride in the back of a pick-up truck on a dirt road near Taiz, amid fighting between Yemeni government forces and Houthis

The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced it will wage an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.

It follows an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days.

The Iran-backed group said it had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco, in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment.

The Yemeni government's fierce statement was expected after the Houthis' offensive last month, which saw them seize control of the country's coastline, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Flames burn at a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh on 3 October

On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory."

Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities.

Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland.

Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi addresses the nation in a televised address in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

But security sources say the Iran-backed Houthis have continued to make gains.

The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.

On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.

Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz.

"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.

Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.

Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil.

On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east.

"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."

It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".

But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.

In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.

On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.

Smoke rises from the site of an air strike in Sanaa on 4 October

Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis.

A war erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital city from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of swathes of the country's north.

Riyadh intervened in the war the following year, leading an international coalition.

After several years of relative calm, the war reignited in July amid the widening conflict in the Middle East.

Last month, a lightning offensive enabled the Houthis to seize the country's entire Red Sea coast, stopping Saudi Arabia from using it as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.

The strategy benefited the Houthis' main sponsor, Iran. But it has also forced Saudi Arabia back into direct military confrontation with the Houthis.

Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control

Watch: BBC reports from the front-line of an escalating war in Yemen

Who are the Houthis and what do they want?

Double strike near crowded market in Yemen

articles.title: Texas Tech fan claims to find part of Colorado's playbook at hotel bar, shows plays that match opening drive
articles.excerpt: "I think that's a concern. I think most, college, you know, most college athletes don't really want to unionize. I think most coaches don't want to have to deal with that. I think most universities an...
articles.body_text:
"I think that's a concern. I think most, college, you know, most college athletes don't really want to unionize. I think most coaches don't want to have to deal with that. I think most universities and athletic departments don't want to have to deal with just one more issue, and it creates a whole new dynamic. And then it then if they're player, then there's tax issues. There's a whole host of things that just aren't necessarily there when we think about college athletics. And so that's a concern that I think some have with the bill. And we're going to take a look at all that when, when we get a chance to deal with the bill in the lame duck session after the election."

A Texas Tech fan claimed to have found pages from Colorado's playbook left behind at a bar inside the hotel where the Buffaloes were reportedly staying ahead of their home matchup against the Red Raiders. Based on the photos shared on social media, the evidence is rather damning for the Colorado coaching staff.

The fan shared the claims to On3's Inside The Double T message board under the name 'VivaTerlingua' on Friday.

"OK I’m not posting pics of it but a bunch of us are in the Colorado team hotel at the bar and we found a 25 page or so playbook that I would bet large amounts of money on is the actual CU playbook," VivaTerlingua posted. "It’s got opening plays, red zone info, our tendencies, etc., etc."

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Will Hammond #15 of the Texas Tech Red Raiders makes a pass against the Colorado Buffaloes at Folsom Field on October 3, 2026 in Boulder, Colorado. (Photo by Chet Strange/Getty Images) (Chet Strange/Getty Images)

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANSION IS NOTHING MORE THAN A DESPERATE FINANCIAL BAILOUT DISGUISED AS PROGRESS

A person who identified themselves as a "buddy" to the group of people who found the alleged pages of the playbook was not as discreet and shared different videos to Instagram showing different pages that appeared to be the same plays Colorado called early on in the game against Texas Tech.

J'Koby Williams #20 of the Texas Tech Red Raiders runs the ball in the third quarter against the Colorado Buffaloes at Folsom Field on October 3, 2026 in Boulder, Colorado. (Photo by Chet Strange/Getty Images) (Chet Strange/Getty Images)

With photos and videos of the alleged playbook made public, another user on X shared a video early Sunday morning that showed the play sheet, and the first six plays of the game from Colorado's offense appeared to match the pages.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

There is no evidence that anyone on the Texas Tech staff received or even saw a copy of the pages from the alleged playbook, but the Red Raiders were lights out against the Buffaloes' offense on Saturday night.

Colorado managed to score on its opening drive of the game, but from then on, the Red Raiders' defense dominated the remainder of the contest.

The Buffaloes threw four interceptions in the second half alone, which helped Texas Tech ultimately cruise to a 29-7 victory to move to 5-0 on the season.

Isaac Wilson #16 of the Colorado Buffaloes drops back for a pass in the fourth quarter against the Texas Tech Red Raiders at Folsom Field on October 3, 2026 in Boulder, Colorado. (Photo by Chet Strange/Getty Images) (Chet Strange/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Despite the fact that, again, there is zero evidence that a Colorado staffer did, in fact, leave a playbook sitting at the hotel bar, the story has taken on a life of its own, and it's not one that puts Colorado head coach Deion Sanders and his program in the brightest of lights amid serious struggles.

Colorado fell to 2-3 on the year with the loss to Texas Tech, and the Buffaloes have been outscored 93-27 over their last three games combined.

articles.title: One southern state's rise is making it America's new 'economic center of gravity'
articles.excerpt:
Texas Stock Exchange strategic adviser and former Rep. Jeb Hensarling breaks down why he believes the Lone Star State is emerging as the nation's next financial powerhouse.

DALLAS — As companies and ...
articles.body_text:
Texas Stock Exchange strategic adviser and former Rep. Jeb Hensarling breaks down why he believes the Lone Star State is emerging as the nation's next financial powerhouse.

DALLAS — As companies and capital flow away from traditional financial hubs like New York and California, one southern state is making an increasingly aggressive bid to become America's next financial powerhouse.

Speaking with Fox News Digital from the Texas Stock Exchange's Dallas headquarters, former Congressman Jeb Hensarling, a strategic advisor to the exchange, said Texas is already becoming "the economic center of gravity in America."

"Texas is really becoming the economic center of gravity in America," Hensarling said.

"As New York is increasingly shoving capital out, Texas is saying, 'You're welcome.' We put out the welcome mat, whereas New York, capital isn't really made to feel at home, and capital wants to go where it's made to feel at home."

AMERICA’S NEXT ECONOMIC POWERHOUSE MAY BE RISING IN RED-STATE TERRITORY

As businesses leave high-cost states, Texas has become the undisputed top destination. (Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News/Getty Images)

The Texas Stock Exchange, which received Securities and Exchange Commission approval last year, is designed to compete with the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq by giving companies another venue to go public and list their shares.

Supporters say the exchange is the latest sign the Lone Star State is evolving from a destination for corporate relocations into a financial center capable of challenging Wall Street.

"Texas has been a great place to do business for decades," Hensarling said. "But increasingly, it's a great place to headquarter your business. Over the last couple of legislative sessions, because of laws passed, it's a great place to incorporate your business. And really the last piece of that puzzle was the Texas Stock Exchange, which is now making Texas the best place to list your company and to go public."

THIS STATE ISN'T JUST GROWING — ITS ECONOMY IS GETTING RICHER PER RESIDENT

The Texas Stock Exchange, which aspires to break off equity listings from Nasdaq and the New York Stock Exchange, is gaining its first converts thanks to Dallas business leaders with close ties to the marketplace. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The exchange has already secured primary listings from companies such as Energy Transfer, Dillard's, Sunoco and Texas Capital Bank. Hensarling said backing from major financial firms such as JPMorgan and BlackRock, along with executives recruited from competing exchanges, demonstrates the venture is more than a branding exercise.

"They don't put their capital in places where they think it's going to lose money," Hensarling said. "It's a lot of validation from the market already."

Hensarling also dismissed criticism that "Y'all Street" is little more than a catchy slogan.

"If it was gimmicky, I'm not really sure the competition would be all of a sudden setting up offices here," he said.

Hensarling pointed to the exchange's financial backers, executives recruited from rival exchanges and companies that have chosen Texas as their primary listing as evidence that it has quickly become a credible competitor.

The Texas Stock Exchange has already announced primary listings from companies such as Energy Transfer, Dillard's, Sunoco and Texas Capital Bank. (Al Drago/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Hensarling said the exchange is simply the latest chapter in Texas' broader economic ascent.

"People are coming to Texas because, again, capital is made to feel welcome," he said. "It's an economic juggernaut... all in all, they're coming here because this is where, economically, the action is."

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title: Subtle change in how you speak could be early sign of dementia risk, new research suggests
articles.excerpt:
Harvard researchers found that people who engaged in moderate amounts of resistance training had a lower risk of dying from several major causes, including heart disease and neurological disease.

New...
articles.body_text:
Harvard researchers found that people who engaged in moderate amounts of resistance training had a lower risk of dying from several major causes, including heart disease and neurological disease.

New research suggests that voice disorders, including shifts in vocal pitch, volume or clarity, could indicate a higher probability of developing dementia or cognitive impairment in the future.

A study involving 833,417 participants aged 50 and older examined the connection between a voice disorder, hearing loss, or both with the chance of developing cognitive impairment or dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, beginning a year after the voice disorder and hearing loss diagnoses.

The findings from the study, conducted by a team at the Drexel University College of Medicine in Philadelphia, were published in the Journal of Voice.

EVERYDAY TASK MAY HELP DETECT EARLY DEMENTIA SIGNS BEFORE DIAGNOSIS, STUDY FINDS

Results showed that participants with a voice disorder but no hearing loss had a 58% increased likelihood of developing dementia or cognitive issues in the future, whereas participants with a voice disorder and hearing loss had a 104% chance.

New research indicates that voice disorders can increase the likelihood of developing dementia in the future. (iStock)

For all participants with voice disorders, with or without hearing loss, there was a 29% increased probability of developing dementia or cognitive impairment, whereas those with only hearing loss had a 27% greater risk.

"We found the strongest link with dementia among patients experiencing a voice disorder and hearing loss," said Robert Sataloff, a professor and chair at the Drexel University College of Medicine, Science Alert reported.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Importantly, we found that those with a voice disorder and no hearing loss were at greater risk than patients who experience hearing loss only," he added.

Examples of voice disorders include laryngitis, vocal cord paralysis, vocal cord lesions and spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia), among others, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

Voice disorders and hearing loss may discourage people from social interaction, which can play a role in dementia development. (Getty Images)

Regardless of the possible correlation between vocal issues and dementia, researchers noted that seeking treatment for a voice disorder could also benefit a patient’s brain.

Hearing loss and trouble speaking could discourage individuals from socializing with others, and studies have shown that social engagement can stimulate the brain and play a role in warding off dementia.

Sataloff said that it’s "only natural" for voice disorders and hearing loss to be connected to cognitive impairment.

Studies have linked hearing loss to an increased risk of dementia. (iStock)

Those who experience pain or discomfort when talking or singing might "participate less often in brain-supporting social or other engaging activities," he noted.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Despite the study's findings, having a voice disorder doesn’t necessarily mean that future cognitive impairment is absolutely certain.

Additionally, it’s not guaranteed that vocal issues indicate the beginning of a decline in brain function or the onset of dementia or Alzheimer’s.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Latino voters swing back to Democrats ahead of midterm elections: poll
articles.excerpt: Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., discusses the GOP's stance on President Donald Trump's immigration policy as the midterm elections approach, weighing in on border security and immigration enforcement on ...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., discusses the GOP's stance on President Donald Trump's immigration policy as the midterm elections approach, weighing in on border security and immigration enforcement on 'America Reports.'

Latino voters are swinging away from President Donald Trump and Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, according to new polling from NBC News and Telemundo.

The poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters across the U.S. from Sept. 21-28, finding that 69% say they disapprove of Trump's performance, compared to just 27% who approve.

Meanwhile, roughly 66% say Trump's deportation policies have gone too far, and 75% say Trump has mishandled the economy and cost of living, the poll found.

FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

The poll likewise found that Democrats hold a huge advantage over the GOP among Latino voters, despite Republicans making gains with the demographic in 2024.

Asked which party they would like to see in control of Congress, 59% of Latino voters said Democrats, compared to 35% who wanted Republicans.

FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

Democrats had just a 12-point lead among Latino voters going into the 2024 elections, showing that Trump and the GOP have lost some of the ground they gained with the voting group.

This screenshot of a Fox News poll indicates that nearly half of respondents believe deportation efforts are too aggressive. (Fox & Friends/Screengrab)

The GOP still shows drastic improvement among Latino voters over the last decade, however. In 2016 and 2018, Latino support for a GOP Congress sat at just 21% and 26% respectively.

LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN

NBC News and Telemundo conducted the poll via phone interviews and online surveys via text message. The poll advertises a margin of error of 3.5%.

The data is the latest in a series of polls showing Democrats have a large advantage over Republicans heading into the midterm elections.

Fox News Power Rankings forecast on the House of Representatives (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Trump argued at a political rally in Dayton, Ohio, on Saturday night that the bad polling numbers have failed to account for his influence on the elections.

"These fake polls, they don't account for one thing. They don't account for the fact that Trump is out campaigning. They never thought this was good. They never thought this was going to happen," Trump told a cheering crowd.

"With you at my side, we have always prevailed and prevailed by a lot and got record-setting votes and record-setting victory," Trump said. "We've won every battle. We've defeated every hope. We've overcome every threat. And now we are on the cusp of beating the communists, socialist, radicalized lunatics and villains once and for all. We're going to put them down once and for all."

In the House of Representatives, Democrats are projected to win 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning the left only needs three more victories out of the 19 possible toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races.

Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

articles.title: Air strike in Sudan kills UN aid truck driver: WFP
articles.excerpt:
An air strike on United Nations trucks has killed a driver in Sudan’s South Kordofan, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

The WFP said in a statement released on Sunday that the trucks,...
articles.body_text:
An air strike on United Nations trucks has killed a driver in Sudan’s South Kordofan, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

The WFP said in a statement released on Sunday that the trucks, carrying food aid, were “clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles” as they came under attack. The agency did not identify those responsible.

The strike hit the convoy on Saturday as it was travelling between two cities controlled by the government’s Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in South Kordofan state.

Fighting in the Kordofan region intensified in late 2025, turning the territory into a strategic battleground between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The two have been fighting for control of Sudan in a civil war that has now lasted more than three years.

The extent of the damage and additional details regarding the attack on WFP aid trucks are still being assessed. The UN agency said that it has called for an investigation.

“These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need,” the statement reads.

Since the war began in April 2023, one in five attacks in Sudan has occurred in the Kordofan region. The army has the upper hand in the north, having made a series of recent gains, while the RSF maintains control over much of the west. South Kordofan remains contested.

Both the SAF and RSF have increasingly deployed drones in their war, with attacks on towns in North Kordofan growing more frequent and deadly, and civilian infrastructure coming under attack across the region.

The civil war has forcibly displaced 14 million people, plunging the country into one of the worst modern food crises and killing tens of thousands of people.

Nearly 19.5 million people – about 41 percent of Sudan’s population – were struggling with acute food crises between February and May, according to an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification assessment, a leading authority on global hunger. More than five million faced extreme, life-threatening food shortages, and 135,000 were at risk of famine.

articles.title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
articles.excerpt:
US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.

Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's...
articles.body_text:
US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.

Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.

She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.

Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."

He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.

He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.

Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday.

"If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."

I interviewed Christa Pike 20 years ago - I can't stop thinking about her

He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement."

"We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]."

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.

She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.

Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges.

Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful.

"I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said.

The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".

Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

How widely used is the death penalty in the US?

Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution

I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's

articles.title: US and Man City’s Cavan Sullivan becomes youngest international goalscorer
articles.excerpt:
Cavan Sullivan became the youngest US international goalscorer in history as the United States defeated archrivals Mexico 3-0 in a friendly international in Arizona on Saturday.

Sullivan, who is pois...
articles.body_text:
Cavan Sullivan became the youngest US international goalscorer in history as the United States defeated archrivals Mexico 3-0 in a friendly international in Arizona on Saturday.

Sullivan, who is poised to join English Premier League side Manchester City next year, netted a superbly taken goal in the 62nd minute to double the USA lead at the State Farm Stadium in Glendale.

At 17 years and five days, Sullivan beat Mathis Albert’s five-day-old record as the youngest US goalscorer.

Albert, aged 17 and 31 days, scored during Tuesday’s 4-2 defeat of Chile.

“These are the moments you dream of when you’re three, four, five or six-years-old,” Sullivan said.

“I manifested this moment, not just these past couple of hours when I found out I was starting, but my whole life,” he added.

Sullivan’s strike came after another teenager — 18-year-old Julian Hall — had given Mauricio Pochettino’s side the lead in the 28th minute.

Hall’s goal was his third in as many games since being handed his international debut by US coach Pochettino in last week’s defeat of Peru. Hall also scored in the victory over Chile.

The loss puts more pressure on Mexico coach Rafael Marquez, who is still seeking his first win since taking over following the World Cup.

Mexico dominated possession and territory early on but were unable to find a way through a well-organised United States defence.

Instead, it was the hosts who took the lead just before the half-hour mark with a superbly worked goal from Hall.

Gio Reyna surged into the penalty area to collect a pass from Alex Freeman and ghosted past Mexico midfielder Erik Lira to reach the byline.

Reyna’s low cross was parried away by Mexico goalkeeper Raul Rangel, but only as far as Hall, who lashed in from close range to make it 1-0.

Mexico’s best chance came early in the second half when Roberto Alvarado’s rasping shot from the edge of the area was tipped over the bar by US goalkeeper Diego Kochen.

Pochettino’s side doubled their lead on 62 minutes when Sullivan’s persistence in chasing down a long ball was rewarded after Rangel mishit a pass to the American outside his area.

Sullivan coolly took his time and chipped home from long range to make it 2-0.

“I just remember chipping the ball, hoping it didn’t hit the crossbar or go over,” Sullivan said of his strike. “I was getting nervous when it was in the air and then everything was a blur.”

A miserable night for Mexico got worse shortly afterwards when substitute Luis Chavez was shown a red card for shoving a hand into the face of Sebastian Berhalter in the 68th minute.

The United States completed the scoring in the 84th minute when Malik Tillman latched onto a poor Mexico backpass and smashed a shot into the top corner for 3-0.

articles.body_text:
